Title: Swing the Front Hand Along a V, Never Higher Than Your Nose
Description: The skating arm swing: a V, not a jogging swing. A certified coach describes a V: the front hand travels forward along an imaginary diagonal and never rises above nose level, while the opposite arm drives straight back and up to make the rear point of the V. Higher than the nose, and the swing lifts you instead of pushing you along. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Opposite Arm Forward to the Leg That Carries You
Description: The arm swing only works when it is tied to the right leg. A certified coach's rule: always swing the opposite arm forward to the leading support leg, the one bearing your weight. Left leg carrying, right hand forward; then it switches. Get it the other way round and the swing fights your balance instead of feeding it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Learn the Arm Rhythm on a One-Leg Push Before You Add Speed
Description: A drill for learning the arm rhythm of skating before you add speed. A certified coach locks the rhythm in with a single-leg push, or the half-lemon drill: one leg does all the pushing, and the opposite arm learns to come forward with every push. Only when that timing is automatic do you build the speed back up. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Arms Swing, Shoulders Stay Still
Description: The arm swing has a limit, and it is the shoulders. A certified coach says: do not twist your torso or rotate your shoulders from side to side. Chest and shoulders stay locked straight ahead, so all the force of the swing goes forward into stride power, none of it sideways into wasted energy. Swinging arms on a still frame is it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: You Pop Up Straight Right After Every Push
Description: Straight knees lock your posture, make you unstable, roll your skates onto the inside edge and set up the backward fall. A certified coach names the moment beginners straighten: right after a push, or during the regroup. Stay continuously low through stride, push and glide — shins into the boot tongue, knees over your toes. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Pizza and Chips on the Grass Before You Touch Tarmac
Description: Staying low on skates: practise on grass before tarmac. A certified coach takes beginners onto grass first: practise the pizza (toes out) and the chips (skates parallel) standing still, in a deep knee bend, where the wheels cannot roll away from you. Then the tarmac — and back to the grass the moment you start rising again. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Hands on Your Knees Until Staying Low Becomes a Habit
Description: Staying low on skates: a hand-on-knee check, not self-talk. A certified coach uses physical targets instead: touch your knees, or rest your hands on them in a ready position, and run constant knee-bend checks while marching and gliding. If your hands can reach your knees, you are low enough; if they cannot, you have popped up. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Quad Transitions: Do Not Swap Your Leading Leg Halfway
Description: On quads, turning from forwards to backwards is a toe or heel flip, and a certified coach names the common mistake: swapping the leading leg mid-transition. It happens because the end position, the backward scissor glide, is not fluent yet. Fix the end first: glide in that scissor until finishing there feels easy. Quad tutorial from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Quad Transitions Are Down, Up, Down With Your Knees
Description: The flip on quads is quick and safe when the wheels you pivot on are unloaded. A certified coach shows a clear down-up-down of the knees: sink, rise just enough to release the heel or toe wheels, flip, and sink again. The fault to watch: coming up and staying up. Practise both sides for eventual fluency. Quad tutorial from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
